c: Current evidence suggests that dinosaur average size varied through the Triassic, Early Jurassic, Late Jurassic and Cretaceous.
def: Size is an important aspect of dinosaur paleontology, of interest to both the general public and professional scientists.

c: Because both modern crocodilians and birds have four-chambered hearts (albeit modified in crocodilians), it is likely that this is a trait shared by all archosaurs, including all dinosaurs.
def: The physiology of non-avian dinosaurs has historically been a controversial subject, particularly their thermoregulation.

def: The scientific question of which larger group of animals birds evolved within has traditionally been called the "origin of birds".

c: Under phylogenetic nomenclature, dinosaurs are usually defined as the group consisting of the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of Triceratops and modern birds (Neornithes), and all its descendants.
def: Birds are vertebrate animals constituting the class Aves, characterised by feathers, toothless beaked jaws, the laying of hard-shelled eggs, a high metabolic rate, a four-chambered heart, and a strong yet lightweight skeleton.

c: In traditional taxonomy, birds were considered a separate class that had evolved from dinosaurs.
def: In biology, taxonomy is the scientific study of naming, defining (circumscribing) and classifying groups of biological organisms based on shared characteristics.

c: Using fossil evidence, paleontologists have identified over 900 distinct genera and more than 1,000 different species of non-avian dinosaurs.
def: Paleontology or palaeontology is the scientific study of the life of the past, mainly but not exclusively through the study of fossils.

c: Dinosaurs are varied from taxonomic, morphological and ecological standpoints. Birds, at over 11,000 living species, are among the most diverse groups of vertebrates.
def: In biology, morphology is the study of the form and structure of organisms and their specific structural features.

c: Birds, at over 11,000 living species, are among the most diverse groups of vertebrates.
def: A species is the basic unit of classification and a taxonomic rank of an organism, as well as a unit of biodiversity.

c: Dinosaurs are represented on every continent by both extant species (birds) and fossil remains.
def: Neontology is a part of biology that, in contrast to paleontology, studies and deals with living organisms.

c: Through most of the 20th century, before birds were recognized as dinosaurs, most of the scientific community presumed dinosaurs to have been sluggish and cold-blooded.
def: A poikilotherm is an animal whose internal temperature varies considerably.

c: Most research conducted since the 1970s, however, has indicated that dinosaurs were active animals with elevated metabolisms and numerous adaptations for social interaction.
def: Metabolism refers to the set of life-sustaining chemical reactions that occur within living organisms.

c: Some were herbivorous, others carnivorous. Evidence suggests that most dinosaurs were egg-laying, and that nest-building was a trait shared by many dinosaurs, both avian and non-avian.
def: A herbivore is an animal anatomically or physiologically evolved to feed on plants, especially upon vascular tissues such as foliage, fruits or seeds, as the main component of its diet.

c: Starting from the 1990s, major discoveries of exceptionally preserved fossils in deposits known as conservation Lagerstätten contributed to research on dinosaur soft tissues.
def: A Fossil-Lagerstätte is a sedimentary deposit that preserves an exceptionally high amount of palaeontological information.

c: Concurrently, a line of work led by Mary Higby Schweitzer, Jack Horner, and colleagues reported various occurrences of preserved soft tissues and proteins within dinosaur bone fossils.
def: John Robert Horner is an American paleontologist best known for his research on dinosaurs.

def: Deinonychosauria is a clade of paravian dinosaurs that lived from the Late Jurassic to the Late Cretaceous periods.

c: Gymnosperm plants (particularly conifers), a potential food source, radiated in the Late Triassic.
def: An evolutionary radiation is an increase in taxonomic diversity that is caused by elevated rates of speciation, that may or may not be associated with an increase in morphological disparity.
